source.title: The Shape of Learning Curves: A Review

record.tranche_reason: The review includes its own PFLD illustration varying feature dimension and training-set size, giving a conceptual test of double-descent and peaking behavior with a different model and setting. Other reviewed results are not counted as this study's own results.
record.gate_note: The review summarizes many results from other work; those cited findings are not rows. Its own Figure 2 varies feature dimension and sample size for PFLD on a toy Gaussian-class problem. Figure 3 describes a separate phase transition, not a reported fall-rise-fall curve. No result on epochs is reported as this study's own.
record.test_reason: Mostly a review of cited work. Its own toy experiments (Figure 2, and Figure 3's 'based on actual experiments' panels) show PFLD, a minimum-norm linear classifier, with sample-wise peaking and a feature-wise double descent. That puts the claim in a non-deep, linear setting. These are illustrations with no numbers, so they are weak evidence. T3 fits better than T2: the setting is new and the figures are not a method aimed at testing the original question.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that learning curves are surprisingly diverse and that no universal parametric model fits them. Ill-behaved curves (peaking/double descent, dipping, and others) can occur even in well-specified, realizable settings. When and why these occur remains poorly understood.
record.recipe_differences: A review that includes an illustrative PFLD toy experiment, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The illustrated error surface and its slices vary with sample size n and feature dimension d'.
record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
record.problems: The own evidence is an illustration on a toy problem and is presented in plots without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The review's broader coverage largely summarizes cited work rather than reporting new tests.
record.rows_left_out: No own result bearing on the claim was left out. The Figure 3 phase-transition illustration is not a reported fall-rise-fall result; cited results throughout the review were excluded.

untested.parts: No deep-network model-size experiment of its own; covered only through cited work.
No epoch-wise result of its own.
Only PFLD on a toy Gaussian problem; no deep networks or real data.
Only one model class (PFLD); the breadth across model classes is not tested by the study's own results.
Regularization removing the peak, noise dependence and multiple peaks are cited (Nakkiran et al., d'Ascoli et al., Skurichina and Duin), not tested.

missing.what: Own PFLD 'Peaking' learning-curve panel: error vs n with a cusp at the under/overparametrized transition. The setup is not detailed in the text; code is in the authors' repository.

record.verdict_notes: The study is a review; nearly all double-descent content is cited and excluded. The study's own evidence is a small set of toy PFLD illustrations built to display known phenomena, without numeric values, repeats or uncertainty. The Figure 3 phase-transition panel is correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: The review discusses deep-network model-wise double descent from cited work but does not test model size in deep networks itself.
The own illustration is a PFLD toy problem, not a test across deep networks or other model classes.
The own capacity-like sweep varies feature dimension for PFLD on one toy problem; it does not establish the pattern across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across axes.
Noise, multiple peaks, and optimally tuned regularization are discussed through cited work, not tested in the review's own results.
No test of whether re-counting complexity turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shape.

rows.subject: pseudo-Fisher's linear discriminant (PFLD)
rows.operation_detail: Varied training-set size while holding feature dimension d' fixed.

conditions.value: toy two-class Gaussian problem; identity covariance matrices; class means distance 6 apart in 100 dimensions, with each dimension contributing equally

rows.note: The figure shows the PFLD learning curve for fixed d'=70. The text says PFLD learning curves can peak around d≈n; the plotted values are not stated numerically.
rows.check: Values and baseline are figure-only. The text says that for this model the largest n is not necessarily best, and the panel is labelled 'Peaking'. No numbers or uncertainty are given.

rows.subject: pseudo-Fisher's linear discriminant (PFLD)
rows.operation_detail: Varied feature dimension d' while holding training-set size fixed.

conditions.value: toy two-class Gaussian problem; identity covariance matrices; class means distance 6 apart in 100 dimensions, with each dimension contributing equally

rows.note: The figure identifies the varying-dimension curve as a feature curve and depicts double descent. The plotted values are not stated numerically.
rows.check: Values are figure-only, and the panel is labelled 'Double Descent'. It is one linear learner on one toy problem. Capacity is feature dimension d', not parameter count against an interpolation threshold, though for PFLD these coincide at d'≈n.

relationships.condition: PFLD without intercept, toy two-Gaussian problem, d'=70, error rate vs n
relationships.reason: The learning curve in Fig. 2b peaks near n≈d' before falling again (R1). This is a figure-only illustration.
relationships.display_finding: Classification error peaked near n ≈ d′, with d′ = 70, before falling with additional samples.

relationships.condition: PFLD feature curve, same toy problem, n=50
relationships.reason: Error falls, peaks near d'≈n, then falls again as d' grows, in a non-deep linear learner (R2). This is a figure-only illustration.
relationships.display_finding: Error initially fell, peaked near d′=n, and fell again as d′ increased.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
